name: Fortran
outlook_would_change_if: Climate, weather and physics codes were rewritten in C++ or Julia at scale.
status_note: Weather, climate and physics codes and the math libraries under NumPy and R keep it in use.
scope_text: FORTRAN I to modern Fortran (2023 standard).
blurb: IBM, John Backus. The first widely used high-level language; still runs weather models and the math libraries under NumPy and R.
description: IBM built Fortran (Formula Translation) in the mid-1950s under John Backus because programming the IBM 704 in assembly was slow and costly. The goal was to let scientists write formulas and still get code as fast as hand-written assembly, and the compiler pulled that off. Its success was the precedent for ALGOL, which was designed as a machine-independent alternative to it. Its strengths are number crunching over large arrays and decades of tuned libraries. Its weaknesses are dated syntax, poor text handling and few new programmers. It still runs weather and climate models, physics simulations and the linear-algebra libraries underneath NumPy, R and MATLAB.
famous_software: BLAS and LAPACK (the reference linear-algebra libraries that NumPy, R and MATLAB ultimately call); WRF (the Weather Research and Forecasting model used by forecasters worldwide); ECMWF IFS (the European Centre's global forecast model, among the most accurate in the world); Parts of SciPy (optimization and special-function routines wrapped for Python)

name: LISP
status_note: McCarthy's LISP and LISP 1.5 are long gone; the family lives on in Common Lisp, Scheme and Clojure.
scope_text: McCarthy's LISP (1958) and LISP 1.5 only; later dialects are drawn separately.
blurb: MIT, John McCarthy. The original LISP (1958) and LISP 1.5: code is data, garbage collection, the REPL. Its living family is drawn as Scheme, Common Lisp and Clojure.
description: John McCarthy designed LISP at MIT in 1958 as a mathematical notation for computation, aimed at artificial-intelligence research; LISP 1.5 (1962) was the first widely used version. Programs and data share one form, nested lists in parentheses, so code can easily write and transform other code, and it introduced garbage collection, the REPL and functions as values. The original language is long gone: this node is the 1958 LISP, and its living family is drawn separately as Scheme, Common Lisp and Clojure (Emacs Lisp is another descendant). Nearly every modern language borrowed something from it, and Landin's ISWIM began as an attempt to free it from lists and brackets.

name: COBOL
organization: CODASYL committee, sponsored by the US Department of Defense
designers: Grace Hopper; Jean Sammet; the CODASYL committee
designer_countries: United States; United States; United States (worked in)
status_note: Billions of lines still run banks and governments; almost nothing new is written.
blurb: Grace Hopper's committee. English-like business language that still processes a large share of bank transactions.
description: COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language) was designed in 1959 by a committee convened by the US Department of Defense, building on Grace Hopper's FLOW-MATIC, to give businesses one portable language for records, money and reports. It reads like English (ADD TAX TO TOTAL), does exact decimal arithmetic and processes huge batches reliably. It is verbose, awkward outside data processing, and its programmers are retiring. Billions of lines still run bank ledgers, insurance, payroll and government benefit systems, mostly on IBM mainframes.
famous_software: Core banking ledgers (account and transaction processing at many of the world's banks); US unemployment systems (state benefit systems that buckled under demand in 2020)

name: ALGOL 60
organization: International committee (meetings in Zurich 1958 and Paris 1960)
status_note: Not used since the 1970s, but its block structure is in nearly every language.
scope_text: ALGOL 60 (with ALGOL 58 as its precursor); ALGOL 68 is drawn separately.
blurb: International committee (ALGOL 58, then ALGOL 60). Block structure and BNF, the grammar notation nearly every later language inherited.
description: ALGOL 60 was designed by an international committee of European and American computer scientists (ALGOL 58, then the 1960 report) as a clean, machine-independent language for describing algorithms. FORTRAN's success was its precedent and John Backus sat on the committee, but the American members deliberately did not base their proposal on IBM's language. It introduced block structure, nested scopes, recursion as standard and the BNF notation still used to define languages. It never became commercially dominant: IBM pushed Fortran, and ALGOL 60 had no standard input and output. It was used mainly in academia and for publishing algorithms, yet CPL, Simula, Pascal and ALGOL 68 descend directly from it, and through them C and Java.
famous_software: Burroughs B5000 MCP (an operating system written in an ALGOL dialect, unusual in 1961)

name: APL
outlook_would_change_if: Dyalog's finance and insurance users moved their array code to Python.
status_note: A small, devoted niche (Dyalog APL, GNU APL); its ideas live on in J, K/q and NumPy.
blurb: IBM, Kenneth Iverson. A math notation turned language; whole-array operations, read right to left.
description: Kenneth Iverson created APL as a mathematical notation at Harvard and turned it into a language at IBM in the 1960s. It works on whole arrays at once with single-character symbols, so a statistical calculation can fit on one line. That makes it extraordinarily concise for exploring data, but it needs a special character set, reads right to left and is famously hard for outsiders to read. It survives in finance and insurance niches (Dyalog APL), its descendants J and K/q (the kdb+ trading databases) are drawn on the map, and its array thinking shaped S, R and NumPy.

name: Pascal
status_note: Free Pascal and Lazarus keep it maintained; it mostly lives on as Delphi.
scope_text: Standard Pascal and Free Pascal; Object Pascal is drawn as Delphi.
blurb: ETH Zurich, Niklaus Wirth. Built to teach structured programming; ancestor of Modula and Oberon.
description: Niklaus Wirth designed Pascal at ETH Zurich around 1970 to teach structured programming clearly and to be easy to compile. It is strongly typed, readable and strict, with records and clean control structures. Standard Pascal was too restrictive for real systems work (no separate compilation, weak strings), gaps that commercial dialects such as Turbo Pascal and Delphi filled. Wirth called ALGOL 60 its precursor, by way of his ALGOL W. Free Pascal and Lazarus keep standard Pascal maintained today. It was the dominant teaching language of the 1970s and 1980s and was used for Apple Lisa and early Mac software and for TeX.
famous_software: TeX (Knuth wrote it in WEB, a literate-programming form of Pascal); Apple Lisa and early Mac apps (Apple's 1980s application code was mostly Pascal)

name: Forth
status_note: Gforth and embedded niches keep it maintained; its idea survives in PostScript. Low confidence: Fading vs. Alive is a close call.
blurb: Chuck Moore. Stack-based, postfix: 2 3 + . The 'German' language, verb last.
description: Chuck Moore developed Forth around 1970 to control radio telescopes at the US National Radio Astronomy Observatory on machines with very little memory. Everything works through a stack in postfix order (2 3 +), and you extend the language by defining new words, so a whole system can be tiny and interactive. That suits small embedded hardware, but the code is hard to read for anyone but its author and the ecosystem is small. It has been used in boot firmware (Open Firmware), spacecraft and embedded controllers, and its idea lives on in PostScript.
famous_software: Open Firmware (boot firmware of Sun workstations and PowerPC Macs, with a Forth prompt)

name: C
outlook_would_change_if: Rust replaced C in new kernels and embedded code much faster than expected.
status_note: Operating systems, databases and embedded devices will run on C for decades; new security-critical code moves to Rust.
blurb: Bell Labs, Dennis Ritchie. Written to build Unix. The source of braces, semicolons and printf.
description: Dennis Ritchie created C at Bell Labs in 1972 to rewrite the Unix operating system in something higher-level than assembly but nearly as fast. It grew out of Ken Thompson's B, to which Ritchie added types, and its type composition owes much to ALGOL 68. It gives direct control over memory through pointers, maps closely to hardware, and has a tiny core with compilers for virtually every chip. That power is also its weakness: manual memory management makes crashes and security holes easy. C runs operating systems, databases, embedded devices and the interpreters of Python and R, and its syntax is the template for C++, Java, JavaScript and Go.
famous_software: Linux kernel (runs Android, most servers and nearly all supercomputers); Unix (C was created to rewrite it); Git (Linus Torvalds's version-control system); SQLite (the most widely deployed database, inside every phone); CPython (the standard Python interpreter); PostgreSQL (the leading open-source relational database); Redis (in-memory data store used for caching)

name: Smalltalk
outlook_would_change_if: Live, image-based environments became an advantage for AI-assisted development.
status_note: Pharo, Squeak and commercial Smalltalks keep a small research and finance niche; its image-based tooling sits awkwardly with file-based workflows.
scope_text: Smalltalk-80 and its descendants Squeak and Pharo (Pharo calls itself 'Smalltalk-inspired').
blurb: Xerox PARC, Alan Kay. Everything is an object that receives messages; also pioneered the GUI. Continues as Squeak and Pharo.
description: Alan Kay's group at Xerox PARC created Smalltalk in the 1970s as a language children and non-specialists could use on personal computers; the same team pioneered the graphical user interface. Everything is an object that receives messages, and you program inside a live environment where anything can be changed while it runs. It is elegant and very productive but lives in its own world (an image file rather than plain text files), which made integration hard and slowed adoption. Squeak and Pharo, its direct descendants, serve research, teaching and some finance systems, and its ideas shaped Objective-C, Java, Ruby, Self and Dart.
famous_software: Squeak and Pharo (live environments where everything can be edited while it runs); JPMorgan Kapital (a derivatives risk system built in the 1990s)

name: Prolog
outlook_would_change_if: LLM-plus-solver systems adopted Prolog widely (upside), or Datalog variants took its place (downside).
status_note: SWI-Prolog and Scryer are active; used in research, rule engines and teaching.
blurb: Marseille, Alain Colmerauer. Logic programming: you state facts and rules, it searches for answers.
description: Alain Colmerauer and colleagues in Marseille created Prolog in 1972 for natural-language processing, building on Robert Kowalski's logic programming. You state facts and rules and Prolog searches for answers that satisfy a query, instead of you writing step-by-step instructions. It excels at rules, parsing and symbolic reasoning but is slow and awkward for numeric or input-heavy programs, and its search can run away unpredictably. It is used in research, teaching, expert systems and language tools, including parts of IBM Watson.
famous_software: IBM Watson (used Prolog to parse questions when it won Jeopardy! in 2011); NASA Clarissa (voice-operated procedure assistant on the International Space Station)

name: ML
status_note: Standard ML (SML/NJ, MLton, Poly/ML) survives in teaching and theorem provers such as Isabelle and HOL4; OCaml and F# carry the line.
blurb: Edinburgh, Robin Milner. The ML line: LCF ML (1973) and Standard ML. Type inference and pattern matching; framework from Landin's ISWIM.
description: Robin Milner created ML (Meta Language) at the University of Edinburgh in 1973 as the scripting language of a theorem prover, a system for proving programs correct. It took its basic framework from Peter Landin's ISWIM and was first implemented in Lisp. It introduced type inference, where the compiler works out every type itself, together with algebraic data types and pattern matching, giving static safety without heavy annotations. As a language it stayed academic, with a small ecosystem and little industry use. This node covers LCF ML and Standard ML (1983, defined 1990), which is used in teaching and proof assistants such as Isabelle and HOL4, and its descendants OCaml and F# and its ideas in Rust, Swift, Scala and Haskell carry it into industry.
famous_software: Isabelle and HOL (theorem provers used to verify mathematics and hardware)

name: SQL
outlook_would_change_if: Natural-language querying turned SQL into an invisible intermediate rather than written code.
status_note: AI writes more SQL than ever, and declarative queries are easy to check.
blurb: IBM, Chamberlin and Boyce. Describe the result, not the loop. Based on Codd's relational model.
description: Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce designed SQL at IBM in 1974 so people could query Edgar Codd's relational databases without writing loops. You describe the result you want (SELECT, FROM, WHERE) and the database decides how to compute it, which makes queries short, optimizable and readable by analysts. Every database speaks a slightly different dialect, complex logic gets clumsy, and procedural work needs extensions such as PL/SQL or T-SQL. It is the universal language of data, from banking systems to BigQuery, Databricks and Power BI.
famous_software: dbt pipelines (analytics transformations written as SQL models); Stored procedures (business logic inside banking and ERP databases)

name: Scheme
outlook_would_change_if: A Scheme (Guile, Chez) became a common embedded or teaching default again.
status_note: Chez, Guile, Gambit and Chicken are maintained; introductory courses in the SICP tradition have mostly moved to Python.
scope_text: The Scheme standards (R5RS–R7RS) and implementations such as Chez, Guile, Gambit and Chicken. Racket, which renamed itself from PLT Scheme in 2010, is not included.
blurb: MIT, Sussman and Steele. A minimal Lisp; the internals R was built on.
description: Gerald Sussman and Guy Steele created Scheme at MIT in 1975 as a minimal, clean dialect of Lisp for exploring models of computation. It has a tiny core with lexical scope, closures and proper tail calls, so a few powerful ideas go a long way, and the textbook SICP made it famous in teaching. Its minimalism led to many incompatible implementations and a small library ecosystem. It is used in teaching, research and as an embedded scripting language (Guile, Chez), and its design shaped JavaScript, R and Lua. Racket, which began as PLT Scheme and renamed itself in 2010, is not part of this node.
famous_software: GNU Guix (a package manager and Linux distribution configured in Guile Scheme); DrRacket (teaching environment used in many introductory courses)

name: S
status_note: Replaced by R; S-PLUS is discontinued.
blurb: Bell Labs, John Chambers. Interactive statistics language; R is its open-source successor.
description: John Chambers and colleagues created S at Bell Labs in 1976 so statisticians could analyze data interactively instead of writing Fortran programs. It treated data, models and graphics as objects you could explore at a prompt, calling fast Fortran routines underneath. Its commercial version, S-PLUS, was expensive and closed, which left room for a free alternative. It was used in statistics departments and industry through the 1990s and won the ACM Software System Award in 1998; R, its open-source successor, has replaced it.
famous_software: S-PLUS (the commercial S system, popular in the 1990s before R took over)

name: MATLAB
organization: University of New Mexico, then MathWorks
outlook_would_change_if: Simulink-centered engineering toolchains kept universities and industry from moving to Python.
status_note: Losing ground to Python in universities and industry.
blurb: Cleve Moler, then MathWorks. Started as an interactive front-end to Fortran linear-algebra libraries.
description: Cleve Moler wrote MATLAB (Matrix Laboratory) in the 1970s at the University of New Mexico so his students could use Fortran linear-algebra libraries without writing Fortran; MathWorks commercialized it in 1984. Moler took its syntax from PL/0, the small Pascal-like language in Wirth's textbook, while the numerics were Fortran's. Everything is a matrix, the syntax is close to mathematical notation, and its toolboxes and Simulink are excellent for engineering and control systems. It is expensive, closed and weaker than Python as a general-purpose language. It is used in engineering, signal processing, control systems and universities, though Python has taken much of its academic ground.
famous_software: Simulink models (control-system designs that generate code for cars and aircraft)

name: Objective-C
status_note: Maintained in older Apple code; Swift has taken over.
blurb: Brad Cox. C plus Smalltalk-style messages; the language of NeXT, macOS and early iPhone apps.
description: Brad Cox and Tom Love created Objective-C in the early 1980s by adding Smalltalk-style messages to C. NeXT, Steve Jobs's company, adopted it, and Apple inherited it for macOS and later iOS. It combines C's speed with dynamic, flexible objects, but its square-bracket syntax is unusual, it is verbose, and it keeps C's memory pitfalls. It was the language of Mac and iPhone apps until Swift took over from 2014, and much of Apple's older code is still Objective-C.
famous_software: WorldWideWeb (Tim Berners-Lee's first web browser, written on a NeXT computer); Cocoa and early iPhone apps (Apple's frameworks and the first App Store generation)

name: C++
outlook_would_change_if: Memory-safety regulation pushed new systems code to Rust much faster.
status_note: Game engines (Unreal), browsers, trading and ML runtimes stay C++; Rust takes some new systems work.
blurb: Bell Labs, Bjarne Stroustrup. C with classes; games, trading systems, browsers.
description: Bjarne Stroustrup created C++ at Bell Labs from 1979 (released 1985) to combine Simula's classes with C's speed. Stroustrup names C, Simula and ALGOL 68 as the only languages that left clear traces in C++ as released in 1985. Its evolution after 1985, including templates (Release 3.0, 1991), drew on ideas from Ada, CLU and ML, and its exception handling on Brian Randell's fault-tolerance work at Newcastle. Templates, classes and automatic resource management let you write high-level code that compiles to fast machine code, which C++ calls zero-cost abstractions. It is huge and complex, easy to misuse, and inherits C's memory-safety problems, so slow builds and security bugs are recurring pain points. It powers game engines, browsers, trading systems, databases, Adobe and Office software and the cores of machine-learning frameworks.
famous_software: Google Chrome (the browser and its V8 JavaScript engine); Unreal Engine (the engine behind Fortnite and many big-budget games); Adobe Photoshop (the standard image editor); Microsoft Office (large parts of Word and Excel); MySQL (open-source database behind much of the early web); PyTorch and TensorFlow cores (the fast engines under the Python interfaces)

name: Excel formulas
outlook_would_change_if: Python in Excel or AI agents took over advanced spreadsheet logic.
status_note: Copilot writes formulas for people who never could; usage keeps growing.
scope_text: The Excel formula language from 1985 to today, including LAMBDA (2020).
blurb: Microsoft. The world's most used programming language, arguably. Since 2020 it even has LAMBDA.
description: Microsoft released Excel in 1985 (first for the Mac), and its formula language grew out of earlier spreadsheets such as VisiCalc and Lotus 1-2-3. Formulas are live: change a cell and everything recalculates, which makes it the most widely used programming environment in the world. Its weaknesses are hidden errors, logic scattered across cells and poor version control; LAMBDA (2020), developed with Microsoft Research's functional-programming team including Haskell co-designer Simon Peyton Jones, finally lets users define their own reusable functions and makes the formula language Turing-complete. It runs budgets, forecasts, financial models and ad-hoc analysis in almost every company.
famous_software: Financial models (budgets, forecasts and valuations in almost every company)

name: Erlang
designers: Joe Armstrong; Robert Virding; Mike Williams
outlook_would_change_if: The BEAM community moved entirely to Elixir and Gleam.
status_note: The BEAM runtime keeps telecom and messaging systems (WhatsApp) running; Elixir draws the newcomers.
blurb: Ericsson. Telecom-grade concurrency and fault tolerance; runs on the BEAM VM. WhatsApp's backend.
description: Joe Armstrong, Robert Virding and Mike Williams developed Erlang at Ericsson in 1986 to program telephone switches that must never go down. It runs millions of lightweight processes that share nothing and pass messages, follows a 'let it crash' philosophy where supervisors restart failed parts, and can upgrade code without downtime. It is excellent for concurrency and fault tolerance but weak at raw number crunching, with an unusual Prolog-like syntax and a small talent pool. It is used in telecoms and messaging (WhatsApp, RabbitMQ), and through Elixir in web back ends.
famous_software: WhatsApp backend (served hundreds of millions of users with a small team); RabbitMQ (widely used message broker); Ericsson AXD301 (telecom switch famous for 'nine nines' reliability)

name: Perl
status_note: Still glues old servers together; new scripting goes to Python.
blurb: Larry Wall. 'There's more than one way to do it.' Regex and text glue for the early web.
description: Larry Wall created Perl in 1987 while working at Unisys, to make report processing and text manipulation easier than combining shell, sed and awk. It made regular expressions a first-class feature and lets you do a lot in very little code, under the motto 'There's more than one way to do it'. That flexibility is also its weakness: Perl code is often hard to read, and the long Perl 6 (Raku) split stalled it. It powered the early web (CGI scripts, IMDb, Booking.com) and survives in system administration, bioinformatics and legacy scripts.
famous_software: IMDb (the movie database ran on Perl in its early years); Booking.com (one of the largest Perl codebases in the world); Bugzilla (Mozilla's bug tracker)

name: Bash
outlook_would_change_if: Agents' shell use stayed in throwaway commands rather than persistent scripts, or Python and declarative CI absorbed scripting.
status_note: Assumption: AI agents run shell commands constantly, and part of that persists as scripts (CI, setup, containers). Running commands is not the same as written code.
blurb: GNU, Brian Fox. 'Bourne Again SHell'. Glues programs together; integer math only.
description: Brian Fox wrote Bash in 1989 for the GNU Project as a free replacement for the Bourne shell, adding command history, line editing and other conveniences. It is the glue of Unix: you combine small programs with pipes, redirections and variables, and it is available on practically every Linux server and Mac. As a programming language it is fragile: quoting rules are treacherous, it only does integer arithmetic and error handling is weak. It runs build, deploy and CI scripts and server administration everywhere, and AI coding agents use it constantly.
famous_software: makepkg (Arch Linux's package-building tool); Build, deploy and CI scripts (the glue of almost every software team)

name: Haskell
outlook_would_change_if: Strong type systems became the preferred target for checking AI-written code.
status_note: Influential and loved, but small: a steep learning curve and a small job market; strong in compilers and finance.
blurb: A research committee. Pure and lazy, with type classes and monads. Pandoc is written in it.
description: A committee of researchers designed Haskell in 1990 to unify the many lazy, purely functional research languages of the 1980s into one open standard. Functions have no side effects, evaluation is lazy, and a strong type system with type classes catches whole classes of bugs before the program runs. The learning curve is steep (monads), performance is hard to predict because of laziness, and the job market is small. It is used in research, compilers, finance and tools such as Pandoc, and its ideas shaped Rust, Scala, Swift, Python and Excel's LAMBDA.
famous_software: Pandoc (document converter behind R Markdown and Quarto); Meta's Sigma (rule engine that fights spam and abuse); ShellCheck (finds bugs in shell scripts)

name: Python
outlook_would_change_if: A faster Python-compatible language or TypeScript took over data and AI tooling.
status_note: The language AI is built in, and the one models write most.
blurb: Guido van Rossum, CWI Amsterdam. Readable, batteries included; now the lingua franca of data.
description: Guido van Rossum created Python at CWI in Amsterdam, starting in 1989 and releasing it in 1991, as a readable scripting language building on his work on ABC. It drew on ABC, C, Modula-3 and C++ for its core design, and later took list comprehensions from Haskell (Python 2.0) and generators from Icon (Python 2.2), while the pandas library brought R-style data frames and SQL-style joins. Mojo (2023) is a Python superset for AI hardware. Indentation-based syntax, a large standard library and an enormous package ecosystem (NumPy, pandas, PyTorch) make it easy to learn and very productive. Pure Python is slow, so speed depends on C extensions, and dynamic typing lets errors slip through to runtime. It dominates data science, machine learning and AI, and is widely used for scripting, automation, web back ends and teaching.
famous_software: Instagram (one of the largest Django deployments in the world); Dropbox desktop client (where Guido van Rossum worked from 2013 to 2019); YouTube (originally written mostly in Python); PyTorch (the leading deep-learning framework, Python on top of C++); Reddit (rewritten from Lisp to Python in 2005)

name: R
outlook_would_change_if: Pharma and academic statistics moved to Python faster (down), or AI made R as easy to write as Python (up).
status_note: Academic statistics, survey methodology, biostatistics and pharma keep R strong; general data work tilts to Python.
blurb: Auckland, Ihaka and Gentleman. S on the outside, Scheme on the inside.
description: Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman created R at the University of Auckland in 1993 as a free implementation of the S language, with Scheme's ideas inside. It is built for statistics: vectors, data frames, formulas and missing values are native, and CRAN offers over 20,000 packages, from mixed models and survey methods to ggplot2. It can be slow and memory-hungry, has quirks from three object systems and is less suited to production software than Python. Its pipe began as %>% in the magrittr package (2014), which credits F#'s |> and Unix pipes; R 4.1 (2021) made |> native syntax, and R core's design note cites magrittr. dplyr's verbs mirror SQL. It is used in academic statistics, biostatistics and pharma, survey research, epidemiology and data journalism.
famous_software: ggplot2 and the tidyverse (Hadley Wickham's grammar of graphics and data tools); Shiny (interactive web apps written in R); Bioconductor (genomics and bioinformatics packages); BBC News graphics (the BBC data team's bbplot style)

name: Java
outlook_would_change_if: Kotlin took over most new JVM work, including back ends.
status_note: A huge enterprise and Android base that will keep running for decades; new JVM work leans to Kotlin.
blurb: Sun, James Gosling. Write once, run anywhere: bytecode on the JVM, garbage collected.
description: James Gosling and his team at Sun Microsystems created Java in 1995, first for consumer devices and then for the web. Code compiles to bytecode that runs on the Java Virtual Machine on any platform, with garbage collection and a large standard library, making it safer than C++ and highly portable. It is verbose, requires ceremony such as a class for everything, and the JVM uses a lot of memory. It runs enterprise back ends, banks, Android apps, big-data systems (Hadoop, Kafka) and Minecraft.
famous_software: Minecraft: Java Edition (the original version of the best-selling game); Apache Hadoop (the open-source big-data platform of the 2010s); Elasticsearch (search engine behind many site searches and log tools); IntelliJ IDEA (JetBrains' IDE, where Kotlin was born); Jenkins (continuous-integration server)

name: JavaScript
outlook_would_change_if: Deployed runtime code were counted instead of newly written source: TypeScript compiles to JavaScript.
status_note: Still what every browser runs, but new code is increasingly written in TypeScript.
blurb: Netscape, Brendan Eich, written in 10 days. Scheme's ideas in Java's clothes.
description: Brendan Eich wrote JavaScript in ten days at Netscape in 1995 to make web pages interactive, borrowing Java's look, Scheme's functions and Self's prototypes. It runs in every browser with no installation, and with Node.js also on servers, giving it the largest developer community in the world. Its rushed design left quirks such as loose type coercion ('1' + 1 is '11') and a confusing 'this', many fixed since 2015. Its ES2015 arrow functions and classes owed much to CoffeeScript (2009), a cleaner syntax that compiled to JavaScript. It runs every interactive website and much server code, increasingly written as TypeScript.
famous_software: Website front-ends (every interactive web page runs JavaScript); Node.js servers (JavaScript on the server since 2009); Google Maps (2005) (showed what AJAX web apps could do)

name: Ruby
outlook_would_change_if: Rails regained its place as the default for new web start-ups.
status_note: Rails keeps it alive (GitHub, Shopify); new projects choose TypeScript or Python.
blurb: Japan, Yukihiro Matsumoto. Designed for programmer happiness; Ruby on Rails.
description: Yukihiro 'Matz' Matsumoto created Ruby in Japan in 1995 as an object-oriented scripting language that puts programmer happiness first. Everything is an object, blocks make code read naturally, and Ruby on Rails (2004) made building web apps dramatically faster. It is slower than many rivals, its flexibility can make large codebases hard to follow, and its popularity has declined since the 2010s. It powers GitHub, Shopify, Basecamp, Homebrew and many startup web apps.
famous_software: GitHub (built on Ruby on Rails); Shopify (one of the largest Rails applications); Homebrew (the Mac package manager); Basecamp (the app Rails was extracted from)

name: PHP
outlook_would_change_if: WordPress lost its share of the web, or modern PHP (Laravel) won back new projects.
status_note: WordPress alone runs a large share of the web; little momentum for new projects.
blurb: Rasmus Lerdorf. Started as personal home-page tools; now runs much of the web, WordPress included.
description: Rasmus Lerdorf created PHP (originally Personal Home Page tools) at the University of Toronto in 1994 and 1995 to manage his website. It embeds directly in HTML and is trivial to deploy on cheap web hosting, which made it the default language of the early web. Its early design was inconsistent and insecure (function naming, type juggling), though PHP 7 and 8 fixed much of this. It powers WordPress, Wikipedia's MediaWiki, the original Facebook and a large share of all websites.
famous_software: WordPress (powers a large share of all websites); MediaWiki (the software behind Wikipedia); Facebook (originally) (later moved to Hack)

name: OCaml
outlook_would_change_if: OCaml's use for verified and analysis tooling grew beyond its niche.
status_note: Finance and compiler niche (Jane Street).
blurb: INRIA, France. ML with objects. Jane Street runs on it; Rust's first compiler was written in it.
description: Xavier Leroy and colleagues at INRIA in France created OCaml in 1996, adding objects and a fast native compiler to the ML family. It combines strong static typing and type inference with practical performance, which makes it excellent for compilers, analyzers and financial systems. Its ecosystem and community are small, multicore support arrived only in 2022, and tooling lagged behind mainstream languages. Its module system follows Standard ML's. It is used at Jane Street, in Meta's code-analysis tools and in proof assistants such as Rocq, and it compiled Rust's first versions.
famous_software: Jane Street trading systems (a trading firm that runs almost entirely on OCaml); Rust's first compiler (used until Rust could compile itself); Flow and Hack type checkers (Meta's tools for JavaScript and Hack); Coq/Rocq (proof assistant used to verify mathematics and compilers)

name: C#
outlook_would_change_if: .NET lost ground on Linux servers, or Unity lost game developers.
status_note: Typed, fast, backed by Microsoft and Unity; a good fit for AI-written code.
blurb: Microsoft, Anders Hejlsberg. Java's rival on .NET's own VM, the CLR.
description: Anders Hejlsberg designed C# at Microsoft in 2000 as the main language of the new .NET platform, Microsoft's answer to Java. It is a typed, modern language that adds features quickly (generics, LINQ queries, async/await) and has excellent tooling in Visual Studio. It was long tied to Windows, although .NET has been open source and cross-platform since 2016, and its ecosystem is more corporate than community-driven. It is used for enterprise back ends, Windows apps, Unity games and web services on Azure.
famous_software: Unity games (including Hollow Knight and Pokémon Go); Stack Overflow (runs on .NET with famously few servers); Roslyn (the C# compiler, written in C#)

name: Scala
outlook_would_change_if: Spark's Scala API regained ground over PySpark and SQL.
status_note: Spark keeps it relevant, but data teams moved to PySpark and SQL.
blurb: EPFL Lausanne, Martin Odersky. Functional plus object-oriented on the JVM. Spark is written in it.
description: Martin Odersky created Scala at EPFL in Lausanne in 2004 to merge object-oriented and functional programming on the Java Virtual Machine. It is concise and expressive, with a powerful type system and full access to Java libraries, which is why Apache Spark and Kafka were written in it. It is complex, compiles slowly, offers many ways to write the same thing, and the move from Scala 2 to 3 split the community. It is used in big-data engineering, financial back ends and some web services, though data teams have largely moved to PySpark and SQL.
famous_software: Apache Spark (the engine under Databricks); Apache Kafka (event-streaming platform; its original broker was in Scala); Akka (toolkit for concurrent, distributed systems); Twitter backend (replaced Ruby on Rails around 2009 to 2011)

name: F#
outlook_would_change_if: Microsoft made F# a first-class choice alongside C#.
status_note: Small, loyal .NET niche.
blurb: Microsoft Research, Don Syme. OCaml's ideas on .NET.
description: Don Syme created F# at Microsoft Research Cambridge in 2005 to bring OCaml-style functional programming to .NET. It offers type inference, immutable data and concise pipelines while using any .NET library, which suits finance and data processing. Its community is small, Microsoft invests far more in C#, and F# developers are hard to hire. It is used in finance, analytics and some back-end systems, and its pipe operator |>, which passes a value into the next function (first seen in Isabelle/ML in 1994), spread from F# to Elixir, OCaml and, through the magrittr package, R.
famous_software: Jet.com pricing engine (e-commerce pricing; Jet.com was later bought by Walmart)

name: Clojure
outlook_would_change_if: REPL-driven development became an advantage for AI agents.
status_note: Loyal users and active releases, but a smaller community than in the mid-2010s; Nubank is its main anchor.
blurb: Rich Hickey. A modern, immutable-by-default Lisp hosted on the JVM.
description: Rich Hickey created Clojure in 2007 as a modern Lisp for the Java Virtual Machine, built around immutable data and safe concurrency. It is concise, interactive (development happens at a live REPL) and can use any Java library. The parentheses, slow JVM start-up and a small hiring pool limit adoption, and the community has shrunk since the mid-2010s. It runs Nubank's banking platform, Datomic and Metabase, and keeps a loyal following.
famous_software: Nubank (Brazil's digital bank, one of the largest Clojure users); Datomic (database built around immutable facts); Metabase (open-source BI tool)

name: DAX
outlook_would_change_if: Power BI and Fabric lost market share, or semantic layers replaced hand-written measures.
status_note: Power BI and Fabric keep growing, but DAX depends on a single vendor's engine.
blurb: Microsoft (Power Pivot, then Power BI). Excel-style formulas evaluated in filter context.
description: Microsoft introduced DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) in 2009 with Power Pivot for Excel; it was built by the Analysis Services team and now drives Power BI. Microsoft describes it as a new formula language extending Excel's, not a subset of MDX, and Jeffrey Wang, its lead developer, says Excel formulas, SQL and MDX were all considered in its design. It looks like Excel formulas but evaluates measures within a filter context, so one formula answers the question for any slice of the data. Filter and row context are hard to master, debugging is limited, and it only works inside Microsoft's tabular engine. It is used to build measures, KPIs and calculated columns in Power BI, Excel and Analysis Services.

name: Go
designers: Robert Griesemer; Rob Pike; Ken Thompson
outlook_would_change_if: Rust or Kotlin took over new cloud infrastructure.
status_note: Runs the cloud; plain code is easy to review when AI writes it.
blurb: Google: Griesemer, Pike, Thompson. Deliberately small; goroutines and channels from Hoare's CSP.
description: Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson designed Go at Google in 2007 (released 2009), frustrated by slow C++ builds and complexity. It is deliberately small, compiles very fast to a single binary, has garbage collection and built-in concurrency with goroutines and channels. It is verbose in places (repetitive error handling), lacked generics until 2022 and is less expressive than Rust or Kotlin. It runs cloud infrastructure such as Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform and Prometheus, plus many back-end services.
famous_software: Docker (packages software into containers); Kubernetes (runs containers across clusters; born at Google); Terraform (infrastructure as code); Prometheus (monitoring and alerting); Hugo (static website generator); CockroachDB (distributed SQL database)

name: Dart
outlook_would_change_if: Flutter became the default for cross-platform apps beyond Google.
status_note: Tied to Flutter's fortunes and to Google's commitment.
blurb: Google Aarhus, Lars Bak. Meant to replace JavaScript; found its role in Flutter (and AngularDart).
description: Lars Bak and Kasper Lund created Dart at Google's Aarhus office in 2011, originally to replace JavaScript in browsers. Other browsers refused to adopt it, but Flutter (2017) gave it a new role: one codebase for iOS, Android, web and desktop apps, with instant hot reload during development. Gilad Bracha's book on Dart names Smalltalk, Java and JavaScript as its main influences: its type checking and mixins follow Strongtalk, its isolates the Erlang actor model, and its async/await C#. Outside Flutter it has almost no use, and its future depends on Google's commitment. It is used for Flutter apps such as Google Pay and BMW's app, and AngularDart powered Google's Ads and Merchant Center web front-ends.
famous_software: Google Pay (rewritten in Flutter); Google Ads app (Flutter mobile app); BMW app (Flutter app for car owners); AngularDart apps (Google's internal web front-ends, Ads and Merchant Center among them)

name: Kotlin
outlook_would_change_if: Kotlin Multiplatform stalled, confining Kotlin to Android.
status_note: Android's default, and Kotlin Multiplatform reaches iOS and servers.
blurb: JetBrains. A pragmatic, null-safe 'better Java'; Android's preferred language since 2019.
description: JetBrains, with Andrey Breslav as lead designer, created Kotlin in 2011 as a pragmatic, more concise replacement for Java on the JVM. It is fully interoperable with Java, null-safe by design and far less verbose, and Google made it Android's preferred language in 2019. It compiles more slowly than Java, and outside Android and JVM back ends its multiplatform story is still maturing. The Kotlin FAQ names Java, C#, JavaScript, Scala and Groovy as inspirations; JavaScript and Groovy are not drawn because no specific transfer has been documented. It is used for most new Android apps, server back ends and Gradle build scripts.
famous_software: Android apps (most new apps, Google's own included); Gradle build scripts (Kotlin DSL for builds); JetBrains IDEs (parts of IntelliJ and its plugins)

name: Julia
designers: Jeff Bezanson; Stefan Karpinski; Viral Shah; Alan Edelman
designer_countries: United States; United States; India; United States
outlook_would_change_if: AI tools defaulted to Julia for numerical code (up), or Python's compilers (Numba, JAX) closed the speed gap (down).
status_note: Strong in climate, pharmaceutical and macroeconomic modeling; AI tools default to Python.
blurb: MIT. As easy as R, as fast as C. Multiple dispatch; strong in scientific computing.
description: Jeff Bezanson, Stefan Karpinski, Viral Shah and Alan Edelman created Julia at MIT in 2012 to solve the 'two-language problem' of prototyping in a slow language and rewriting in a fast one. It is as easy as Python or R yet compiles to fast code, with multiple dispatch and excellent numerical support. Slow start-up and compile latency, fewer mature packages and a small job market have held it back. It is used in climate modeling, pharmaceutical modeling, optimization and scientific research.
famous_software: CliMA (Caltech-led climate model); Pumas (drug-dosing models used in pharma); NY Fed DSGE model (the New York Fed's macroeconomic model)

name: TypeScript
outlook_would_change_if: Native type annotations in JavaScript made TypeScript's compiler unnecessary.
status_note: GitHub's most used language since 2025; types make AI-written code safer.
blurb: Microsoft, Anders Hejlsberg. JavaScript plus a structural type system; GitHub's most used language in 2025.
description: Anders Hejlsberg led the design of TypeScript at Microsoft in 2012 to make large JavaScript codebases manageable. It adds optional static types to JavaScript and compiles to plain JavaScript, catching errors before code runs and giving editors excellent autocomplete. Its type system is structural and erased at runtime, unlike C#'s, although both were designed under Hejlsberg. It is complex, it needs a build step, and types disappear at runtime, so they guarantee nothing about incoming data. It became GitHub's most used language in 2025 and is used for web front-ends (Angular, React), Node.js servers and tools such as VS Code and Claude Code.
famous_software: Visual Studio Code (Microsoft's open-source editor); Angular (Google's web framework); Claude Code (Anthropic's coding agent); Slack desktop app (Electron app written in TypeScript)

name: Elixir
outlook_would_change_if: Its gradual type system and Phoenix drew a much larger community.
status_note: A loved niche for real-time back ends; a small community and public codebase.
blurb: José Valim. Ruby-like syntax on Erlang's BEAM VM.
description: José Valim created Elixir in Brazil in 2012 to bring a friendly, Ruby-like syntax and modern tooling to Erlang's battle-tested virtual machine. It inherits Erlang's lightweight processes and fault tolerance and adds macros, an excellent package manager and the Phoenix web framework. It is not suited to heavy number crunching, its community is small, and dynamic typing (a gradual type system is arriving) limits tooling. José Valim says its pipe operator came from F#. It is used for real-time systems, chat and messaging (Discord) and web back ends.
famous_software: Discord (real-time messaging for millions of users); Phoenix (web framework with live-updating pages)

name: Power Query M
outlook_would_change_if: Power Query were replaced by Python or SQL in Fabric.
status_note: Lives as long as Power Query in Excel and Power BI, even if people increasingly click or prompt rather than type it.
blurb: Microsoft. Functional, lazy, case-sensitive language behind Power Query's Applied Steps.
description: Microsoft created the M language in 2013 for Power Query, first as an Excel add-in and now in Power BI and Fabric. Microsoft describes it as 'similar to F#': a functional, partly lazy language in which each step transforms a table, and most users generate it by clicking in the Power Query editor without ever seeing the code. Writing it by hand is awkward, it is case-sensitive unlike DAX, and performance tuning (query folding) is opaque. It is used to import, clean and reshape data before modeling in Excel and Power BI.

name: Swift
outlook_would_change_if: Swift gained real server-side or cross-platform adoption (up), or Apple shifted to another language (down).
status_note: Apple's future, but bounded by Apple's platforms.
blurb: Apple, Chris Lattner (also LLVM's creator). Replaced Objective-C; safe by default.
description: Chris Lattner started Swift at Apple in 2010 (released 2014) to replace Objective-C with a modern, safe and fast language. It has type inference, optionals instead of null pointers, value types and concise syntax, and compiles through LLVM to fast code. It is tied mostly to Apple's platforms, compile times can be slow, and the language changed rapidly in its early years. Lattner names Objective-C, Rust, Haskell, Ruby, Python, C# and CLU as sources of ideas; the map draws links only where a transfer can be identified. Its later ownership features (Swift 5.9) follow Rust, and Rust in turn took optional bindings from Swift. It is used for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Watch and Vision Pro apps, plus some server-side code.
famous_software: iPhone and Mac apps (most new ones); SwiftUI (Apple's declarative UI framework)

name: Rust
organization: Personal project from 2006, then Mozilla Research (announced 2010)
outlook_would_change_if: Memory-safety requirements relaxed, or C++ safety profiles won back new systems work.
status_note: The memory-safety push plus a compiler that checks AI-written code.
blurb: Graydon Hoare's personal project from 2006, announced by Mozilla in 2010; version 1.0 in 2015. Memory safety without a garbage collector, checked by the borrow checker.
description: Graydon Hoare started Rust as a personal project in 2006; Mozilla sponsored it from 2009, announced it in 2010 and version 1.0 arrived in 2015. The Rust Reference lists its influences: SML and OCaml, C++, Cyclone, Haskell, Newsqueak, Alef and Limbo, Erlang, Swift, Scheme, C# and Ruby; its first compiler was written in OCaml. Its ownership and borrowing rules, checked at compile time, give memory safety without a garbage collector, so it is as fast as C++ while avoiding most of its crashes and security holes. The learning curve is steep, compile times are long and the borrow checker rejects many programs at first. It is used for systems software, Firefox, cloud infrastructure, the Linux kernel, command-line tools and fast Python libraries (Polars, uv, Ruff).
famous_software: Firefox Stylo (parallel CSS engine); Linux kernel drivers (Rust was accepted into the kernel in 2022); Polars (fast DataFrame library for Python); uv and Ruff (Python package manager and linter); Cloudflare Pingora (proxy handling a large share of web traffic); AWS Firecracker (micro-VMs behind AWS Lambda)

name: Simula
status_note: Unused, but every class you write descends from it.
blurb: Norwegian Computing Center, Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard. The first object-oriented language: classes, objects, inheritance.
description: Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard created Simula at the Norwegian Computing Center in the 1960s (Simula 67) to write simulations, as an extension of ALGOL 60. It invented classes, objects, inheritance and virtual methods, the foundation of object-oriented programming. It was slow on the hardware of its day and never gained wide commercial use. It was used for simulation and teaching, mainly in Scandinavia, and Dahl and Nygaard won the 2001 Turing Award because C++, Smalltalk and Java grew from it.

name: BCPL
status_note: Martin Richards still maintains a distribution; no new projects. Lives on through C.
blurb: Cambridge, Martin Richards. A stripped-down CPL that became B and then C. 'hello, world' first appeared in a tutorial for its descendant B.
description: Martin Richards designed BCPL at the University of Cambridge in 1967 as a simplified version of CPL that was easy to compile and port. It had a single data type (the machine word) and braces for blocks, which kept it small and portable, at the cost of any type safety. It was used for compilers, the Xerox Alto's software and early games such as MUD. Ken Thompson's B stripped it down further, and B became C.
famous_software: Xerox Alto software (the 1973 computer that pioneered the graphical interface); MUD1 (the first multi-user dungeon game, rewritten in BCPL)

name: CLU
status_note: Research language; its iterators are everywhere.
blurb: MIT, Barbara Liskov. Data abstraction, iterators with yield, multiple return values. Liskov won the 2008 Turing Award.
description: Barbara Liskov and her students at MIT created CLU in 1974 to explore data abstraction: defining new types by what they do rather than how they are built. It introduced iterators with yield, multiple return values and exceptions in a clean form. It remained a research language without industrial adoption. Its ideas shaped Ada, C++, Python, Ruby, Lua and Swift, and Liskov received the 2008 Turing Award partly for it.

name: AWK
designers: Alfred Aho; Peter Weinberger; Brian Kernighan
outlook_would_change_if: Its one-liner role moved entirely to Python and AI-generated scripts.
status_note: Still on every Unix machine for one-liners.
blurb: Bell Labs: Aho, Weinberger, Kernighan (the name is their initials). Pattern-action text processing on the command line.
description: Alfred Aho, Peter Weinberger and Brian Kernighan created AWK at Bell Labs in 1977; the name is their initials. It processes text line by line: for every line matching a pattern, it runs an action, with built-in fields and associative arrays. It is perfect for one-liners but awkward for anything large. It is still on every Unix-like system for reports and log processing, and it inspired Perl.

name: Bourne sh
outlook_would_change_if: POSIX sh stopped being the portable default for system scripts.
status_note: Lives on as POSIX sh, the shell every script can count on.
scope_text: The Bourne shell and the POSIX sh standard based on it; Bash is drawn separately.
blurb: Bell Labs, Stephen Bourne. The Unix shell that Bash re-implements; its keywords came from ALGOL 68.
description: Stephen Bourne wrote the Bourne shell at Bell Labs in 1979 for Version 7 Unix, replacing Ken Thompson's simpler shell with a real scripting language. It added variables, functions and control structures with ALGOL 68-style keywords (if ... fi, case ... esac), turning shell scripts into programs. It is minimal and full of quoting pitfalls, but as the POSIX sh standard it runs everywhere. It is used for portable scripts and system start-up, and Bash, Zsh and Dash descend from it.
famous_software: Unix startup scripts (booted classic Unix systems)

name: Ada
organization: CII Honeywell Bull, for the US Department of Defense
outlook_would_change_if: Rust displaced Ada in safety certification (avionics, rail).
status_note: Avionics, rail and defense certify on Ada; Rust is entering the same safety niche.
blurb: CII Honeywell Bull for the US Department of Defense, led by Jean Ichbiah. Strong typing, generics, exceptions; still used in avionics.
description: Jean Ichbiah's team at CII Honeywell Bull in France designed Ada (1980) after the US Department of Defense ran a competition to replace the hundreds of languages used in its systems. Named after Ada Lovelace, it emphasizes strong typing, modules, generics and concurrency, catching errors at compile time in software that must not fail. It is verbose, compilers were long expensive, and few developers know it outside its niche. Its manual names the Pascal family as Ada's main source, with ALGOL 68, Simula, Alphard and CLU as lesser influences. It is used in avionics (Boeing 777), rail signaling, air-traffic control, defense and space, and its syntax shaped Oracle's PL/SQL.
famous_software: Boeing 777 (flight-control software); Paris Métro Line 14 (driverless train control); Air-traffic control (several European systems)

name: Miranda
status_note: Superseded by Haskell; its source was released in 2020.
blurb: University of Kent, David Turner. Lazy and pure; Haskell was created partly because Miranda was proprietary.
description: David Turner created Miranda at the University of Kent in 1985 as a lazy, purely functional language with a clean, mathematical syntax. It made lazy evaluation and polymorphic types practical and pleasant to use. It was a commercial product with a license fee, which pushed researchers to design an open alternative, Haskell. It was used in teaching and research in the late 1980s and is now historical, though Haskell's syntax owes it a great deal.

name: ABC
designers: Leo Geurts; Lambert Meertens; Steven Pemberton
status_note: Superseded by Python.
blurb: CWI Amsterdam: Geurts, Meertens, Pemberton. A teaching language; Guido van Rossum worked on it before creating Python.
description: Leo Geurts, Lambert Meertens and Steven Pemberton designed ABC at CWI in Amsterdam in the 1980s as a teaching language to replace BASIC. It had indentation-based blocks, a few powerful built-in types (lists, dictionaries) and an integrated environment. It was too closed to catch on, because it could not easily work with files or the operating system. It is remembered as Python's parent: Guido van Rossum worked on ABC before creating Python.

name: Self
status_note: Still maintained by its authors, but no new projects; lives on in JavaScript's prototypes and in JIT techniques.
blurb: Xerox PARC and Stanford, David Ungar and Randall Smith. Objects without classes (prototypes); its fast VM techniques later fed Java's HotSpot.
description: David Ungar and Randall Smith created Self at Xerox PARC in 1987, continuing it at Stanford and Sun, as a simpler Smalltalk without classes: new objects are made by copying prototypes. Its research team invented adaptive just-in-time compilation techniques that made dynamic languages fast. It never left the research lab, although its authors still maintain it. Its prototypes live on in JavaScript, and its compiler techniques went into Java's HotSpot JVM and Chrome's V8.

name: Oberon
status_note: Academic; lives on through Go.
blurb: ETH Zurich, Niklaus Wirth and Jürg Gutknecht. Successor of Pascal and Modula-2; Robert Griesemer did his PhD on it before co-creating Go.
description: Niklaus Wirth and Jürg Gutknecht created Oberon at ETH Zurich in 1987 as both a language and a complete operating system, written by the two of them. It took Modula-2 and removed everything nonessential, to show that a whole system can be simple and understandable. It stayed academic, with few users outside ETH. It was used for teaching and research, and it influenced Go through Robert Griesemer, who wrote his doctorate on an Oberon extension.
famous_software: Oberon OS (a complete operating system written by two people at ETH)

name: Dartmouth BASIC
status_note: Line-numbered classic BASIC is gone; its heirs are VB and VBA.
scope_text: Dartmouth BASIC and the classic line-numbered BASICs; Visual Basic and VBA are drawn separately.
blurb: Dartmouth College, John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz. The original BASIC for students; its heirs are drawn separately (Visual Basic, VBA).
description: John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz created Dartmouth BASIC (Beginner's All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code) at Dartmouth College in 1964 so that non-science students could use time-sharing computers. It was simple to learn, with line numbers and plain commands, and it was built into almost every home computer of the 1970s and 1980s. Classic BASIC encouraged tangled GOTO code, which Dijkstra famously criticized, and had no structure for large programs. It taught a generation to program, was Microsoft's first product, and its heirs Visual Basic and VBA are drawn separately.
famous_software: Altair BASIC (Microsoft's first product, 1975); Home computers (the built-in language of the C64, ZX Spectrum and Apple II)

name: Logo
designers: Wally Feurzeig; Seymour Papert; Cynthia Solomon
designer_countries: United States; South Africa; United States
status_note: Implementations survive, but its classroom role passed to Scratch.
blurb: BBN and MIT: Wally Feurzeig, Seymour Papert, Cynthia Solomon. 'Lisp without parentheses' for children, with the drawing turtle.
description: Wally Feurzeig, Seymour Papert and Cynthia Solomon created Logo at BBN and MIT in 1967 to teach children mathematical thinking. It is essentially Lisp without parentheses, best known for turtle graphics, where children steer a turtle to draw shapes. It was seen as a children's language and had little use outside education. It shaped educational computing worldwide and led directly to Scratch.

name: Visual Basic
status_note: VB6 is long gone and VB.NET has been frozen since 2020; VBA is drawn separately.
scope_text: Visual Basic 1–6 and VB.NET; VBA is drawn separately.
blurb: Microsoft, after Alan Cooper's prototype. Drag buttons onto a form, then write BASIC behind them; lives on as VBA in Office.
description: Microsoft released Visual Basic in 1991, building on Alan Cooper's visual form designer: you drew windows with buttons and wrote BASIC code behind them. It made Windows programming accessible to millions and popularized rapid application development. It tended to produce hard-to-maintain code, VB.NET (2002) broke compatibility with VB6, and Microsoft stopped evolving the language in 2020. VBA, drawn separately, carries it on in Office.
famous_software: Windows business apps (countless 1990s in-house tools)

name: Delphi
outlook_would_change_if: Embarcadero's cross-platform tooling won new projects.
status_note: Top 15 on TIOBE thanks to long-lived business apps; few new projects.
scope_text: Delphi's Object Pascal, from Borland to Embarcadero.
blurb: Borland, chief architect Anders Hejlsberg. Visual Object Pascal: Visual Basic's ease with compiled speed.
description: Borland released Delphi in 1995, with Anders Hejlsberg as chief architect, as an Object Pascal environment for building Windows applications visually. It combined Visual Basic's drag-and-drop ease with fast, compiled native programs and a rich component library. Borland's decline, high license costs and the rise of .NET and the web reduced it to a niche. It is used for long-lived business applications and tools such as FL Studio and Total Commander, and Skype's first Windows client was written in it.
famous_software: Skype (the original Windows client); FL Studio (music production software); Total Commander (two-pane file manager)

name: Lua
designers: Roberto Ierusalimschy; Luiz Henrique de Figueiredo; Waldemar Celes
outlook_would_change_if: Roblox's Luau or game engines moved to another scripting language.
status_note: Roblox, games and Neovim; tiny and easy to embed.
blurb: PUC-Rio, Brazil: Ierusalimschy, de Figueiredo, Celes. Tiny and embeddable; scripting in games, Roblox and Neovim.
description: Roberto Ierusalimschy, Luiz Henrique de Figueiredo and Waldemar Celes created Lua at PUC-Rio in Brazil in 1993, first for Petrobras engineering tools. It is tiny, fast and designed to be embedded inside other programs, with a single flexible data structure, the table. Its authors name Modula, CLU, C++, SNOBOL and Awk, and C as the sources of Lua 1.0; Scheme came later, with closures in Lua 3.1 (1998) and full lexical scoping in Lua 5.0 (2003). Its standard library is minimal, arrays start at 1 and it lacks the large ecosystem of Python. It is used for game scripting (Roblox, World of Warcraft add-ons), Neovim configuration and embedded devices.
famous_software: Roblox (games written in Luau, a Lua dialect); World of Warcraft add-ons (player-written interface mods); Neovim (the editor's plugins and configuration); Adobe Lightroom (large parts of its interface logic)

name: Scratch
outlook_would_change_if: AI tutors replaced block-based first steps in schools.
status_note: How millions of children start coding; AI tutors may change that.
blurb: MIT Media Lab, Mitchel Resnick's group. Programming by snapping blocks together; first built in Squeak Smalltalk.
description: Mitchel Resnick's Lifelong Kindergarten group at the MIT Media Lab released Scratch in 2007 so children could make games and stories by snapping visual blocks together. It removes syntax errors entirely and encourages sharing and remixing in an online community of millions. It is limited for larger programs and is meant as a first step rather than a professional tool. It is used in schools and coding clubs worldwide as many children's first programming language.

name: Zig
organization: Independent, now the Zig Software Foundation
outlook_would_change_if: Zig stalled before 1.0, or Rust absorbed the 'better C' niche.
status_note: A simpler 'better C' with growing adoption, but still before version 1.0.
blurb: Andrew Kelley. A simpler, safer replacement for C with no hidden control flow. The Bun JavaScript runtime is written in it.
description: Andrew Kelley created Zig in 2016 as a simpler, safer replacement for C. It has no hidden control flow or hidden memory allocations, powerful compile-time code execution, and it can compile and cross-compile C code with ease. It has not reached version 1.0, breaking changes are common and the ecosystem is young. It is used for performance-critical tools such as the Bun JavaScript runtime, the TigerBeetle database and the Ghostty terminal.
famous_software: Bun (fast JavaScript runtime); TigerBeetle (financial-transactions database); Ghostty (terminal emulator)

name: PL/I
status_note: Still runs on IBM mainframes; nothing new is written in it.
blurb: IBM, led by George Radin. Meant to merge Fortran's science and COBOL's business data in one language; Multics was written in it.
description: IBM designed PL/I (Programming Language One) from 1964, with its users' group SHARE, to replace both Fortran and COBOL with one language for the new System/360. It combined scientific computing, business records, exception handling and multitasking. It was enormous and hard to compile, so it never displaced either parent. It was used for Multics and IBM mainframe applications, some of which still run, and early SAS was written partly in it.
famous_software: Multics (the 1960s operating system that inspired Unix)

name: SPSS
designers: Norman Nie; Dale Bent; Hadlai Hull
designer_countries: United States; United States (worked in); United States (worked in)
outlook_would_change_if: IBM invested in SPSS syntax again, or point-and-click analysis regained ground.
status_note: Point-and-click users in social science and market research; syntax users drift to R and Python.
blurb: Stanford: Norman Nie, Dale Bent, Hadlai Hull. Command syntax for social-science statistics; owned by IBM since 2009.
description: Norman Nie, Dale Bent and Hadlai Hull created SPSS (Statistical Package for the Social Sciences) at Stanford in 1968 so social scientists could analyze surveys without programming in Fortran. It was first written in Fortran. Its syntax is a sequence of English-like commands with DO IF, LOOP and a macro facility, which makes analyses reproducible, and its menus make it accessible to non-programmers. It is expensive, closed (owned by IBM since 2009) and much less flexible than R or Python. It is used in social science, psychology, market research and survey analysis.

name: SAS
organization: North Carolina State University, then SAS Institute
designers: Anthony Barr; James Goodnight; John Sall; Jane Helwig
designer_countries: United States; United States; United States; United States
outlook_would_change_if: Regulators and pharma kept SAS as the default for submissions.
status_note: Entrenched in pharma and banking, but the FDA now accepts R and licenses are expensive.
blurb: North Carolina State University: Anthony Barr, James Goodnight, John Sall, Jane Helwig. DATA steps and PROCs; the standard in pharma for decades.
description: Anthony Barr, James Goodnight, John Sall and Jane Helwig developed SAS at North Carolina State University from 1966 to analyze agricultural research data; SAS Institute was founded in 1976. Early SAS was written partly in PL/I. Its DATA steps and PROCs process very large datasets reliably, and its validated procedures became the standard for regulatory work. Licenses are expensive, the language is idiosyncratic, and talent is shifting to R and Python. It is used in pharmaceutical clinical trials, banking, insurance and government statistics.
famous_software: Clinical-trial analyses (decades of drug-approval submissions to regulators)

name: Stata
outlook_would_change_if: Applied economics kept teaching Stata as the default.
status_note: Still the default in applied economics; slowly losing students to R and Python.
blurb: William Gould, later StataCorp in Texas. Do-files, ado-files and the Mata matrix language; the default in applied economics.
description: William Gould created Stata in 1985 at the Computing Resource Center (now StataCorp) to give researchers fast, reliable econometric tools. Its command syntax is concise and consistent, the documentation is outstanding, and it handles panel data, survey data and regression extremely well, with Mata, a C-like matrix language added in Stata 9 (2005). It is commercial, traditionally works with one dataset in memory at a time and is less flexible than R for graphics and custom methods. It is used in applied economics, public health, political science and policy research.

name: ABAP
outlook_would_change_if: SAP moved custom development off ABAP.
status_note: Runs SAP systems worldwide, and SAP keeps it alive as ABAP Cloud.
blurb: SAP, Walldorf. The language of SAP's business systems; reads a lot like COBOL.
description: SAP created ABAP in 1983 as a report language for its R/2 mainframe software, and it became the language of all SAP business applications. It is tightly integrated with SAP's database and business objects, so finance, logistics and HR processes can be customized inside the system. It is verbose and COBOL-like, useful only inside SAP, and its developers are a specialized pool. It is used to customize and extend SAP ERP and S/4HANA at large companies worldwide.
famous_software: SAP S/4HANA (ERP software running finance and logistics at large companies)

name: Modula-3
organization: DEC Systems Research Center and Olivetti Research
designers: Luca Cardelli; Greg Nelson; Bill Kalsow; Jim Donahue; Mick Jordan
designer_countries: Italy; United States; United States (worked in); United States (worked in); United States (worked in)
status_note: Academic; lives on through Python.
blurb: DEC Systems Research Center and Olivetti Research. A safer, object-oriented successor of Modula-2; Python took its module, exception and class design from it.
description: A team at Digital Equipment Corporation's Systems Research Center and Olivetti Research designed Modula-3 in 1988 as a safer, object-oriented successor to Wirth's Modula-2. It combined modules, objects, exceptions, garbage collection and threads in a clean, simple language. It had no corporate champion after DEC's decline and never gained a user base. It is remembered for its influence on Python's modules, exceptions and classes, and on parts of Java's design.

name: Hack
designers: Julien Verlaguet; Alok Menghrajani; Drew Paroski
designer_countries: France; United States (worked in); United States (worked in)
outlook_would_change_if: Hack spread beyond Meta and a few companies such as Slack.
status_note: Used almost only inside Meta and a few companies such as Slack.
blurb: Meta (Facebook). PHP with gradual static typing, running on Meta's HHVM engine.
description: Meta (then Facebook) created Hack in 2014, with Julien Verlaguet among its lead designers, to add static types to its enormous PHP codebase without stopping development. It adds gradual typing, generics and async functions to PHP and runs on Meta's HHVM virtual machine, with a type checker written in OCaml. Outside Meta it has little adoption, and it has diverged from mainstream PHP. It runs Facebook's and Messenger's web back ends, and Slack migrated its back end to Hack.
famous_software: Facebook backend (the web tier of Facebook and Messenger); Slack backend (migrated from PHP to Hack)

name: PowerShell
outlook_would_change_if: Windows and Azure administration moved to another automation language.
status_note: Windows and Azure administration depend on it.
blurb: Microsoft, Jeffrey Snover. A shell where commands pass .NET objects to each other instead of plain text.
description: Jeffrey Snover led the creation of PowerShell at Microsoft in 2006 to give Windows a powerful command-line automation tool. Unlike Unix shells, its commands pass structured .NET objects through pipelines rather than plain text, with consistent verb-noun names such as Get-Process. It is verbose and slower to start than Bash, and on Linux it remains a minority choice. It is used to administer Windows servers, Active Directory, Azure and Microsoft 365.
famous_software: Windows Server and Azure automation (how administrators script Microsoft's cloud and servers); Microsoft 365 administration (user, mailbox and license management at scale)

name: Mathematica
outlook_would_change_if: AI assistants replaced symbolic computation for researchers.
status_note: Entrenched in physics and math research; AI assistants compete for casual use.
scope_text: Mathematica's language, now called the Wolfram Language.
blurb: Wolfram Research, Stephen Wolfram. The Wolfram Language: symbolic math, notebooks and built-in knowledge.
description: Stephen Wolfram released Mathematica in 1988 through Wolfram Research; its language is now called the Wolfram Language. Wolfram says his early sketches for SMP, its predecessor, looked like LISP and APL before he invented his own design. Everything is a symbolic expression, so it handles algebra, calculus and exact mathematics as well as numerics, with thousands of built-in functions and curated data. It is proprietary and expensive, and its unusual syntax rarely leaves its notebooks. It is used in physics, mathematics and engineering research and in education, it powers Wolfram|Alpha, and its notebook interface inspired Jupyter.
famous_software: Wolfram|Alpha (the computational answer engine); Mathematica notebooks (the notebook format that inspired Jupyter)

name: TeX
outlook_would_change_if: Mathematics and physics publishing moved to another typesetting system (e.g. Typst).
status_note: Still how mathematics and physics are typeset; Overleaf keeps it current.
scope_text: TeX and the macro packages built on it, such as LaTeX.
blurb: Stanford, Donald Knuth. A typesetting system that is also a full programming language; LaTeX is built on it.
description: Donald Knuth created TeX at Stanford in 1978 because he was unhappy with the typesetting of his book series The Art of Computer Programming. Knuth wrote it in WEB, his literate-programming system built on Pascal. It produces superb typography, especially for mathematics, and is a full, if odd, macro programming language; Leslie Lamport's LaTeX (1984) made it practical for authors. Error messages are cryptic, macros are hard to debug and the layout is not visual. It is the standard for mathematics, physics and computer-science papers, theses and books.
famous_software: LaTeX (Leslie Lamport's macro package that most people actually use); arXiv papers (most mathematics and physics preprints); The Art of Computer Programming (Knuth created TeX to typeset it)

name: Modula-2
status_note: A GCC front end keeps it compilable; mostly historical.
blurb: ETH Zurich, Niklaus Wirth. Pascal plus modules, designed for the Lilith workstation.
description: Niklaus Wirth designed Modula-2 at ETH Zurich in 1978 as the successor to Pascal, to write the operating system of the Lilith workstation. Its key addition was modules with separate compilation and clear interfaces, which made Pascal-style programming suitable for large systems. It was overshadowed by C, C++ and Turbo Pascal's popular extensions. It was used in teaching and some embedded and industrial systems, and it led to Oberon and Modula-3.
famous_software: Lilith (ETH's workstation, with its operating system written in Modula-2)

name: Eiffel
status_note: A small commercial niche; its ideas live on in other languages.
blurb: Interactive Software Engineering, Bertrand Meyer. Object-oriented with 'design by contract': routines declare what they require and guarantee.
description: Bertrand Meyer created Eiffel in 1986 at Interactive Software Engineering in California to make object-oriented software reliable. Its central idea is design by contract: routines state preconditions, postconditions and invariants that are checked as the program runs. It has a small community, commercial tooling and little industry adoption. It is used in teaching (Meyer later taught at ETH Zurich) and in some finance and defense systems, and its ideas influenced C#, Java and Ruby.

name: Icon
status_note: Research language; its generators live on in Python.
blurb: University of Arizona, Ralph Griswold. Goal-directed evaluation and generators; successor of SNOBOL.
description: Ralph Griswold created Icon at the University of Arizona in 1977 as the successor to SNOBOL, for text and string processing. Its expressions can generate a series of results and backtrack automatically when one fails, a style called goal-directed evaluation. It remained a niche research language. Its generators directly inspired Python's yield.

name: SNOBOL
designers: David Farber; Ralph Griswold; Ivan Polonsky
designer_countries: United States; United States; United States (worked in)
status_note: SNOBOL4 implementations survive; no new projects. Its pattern matching lives on in AWK, Icon and regular expressions.
blurb: Bell Labs: Farber, Griswold, Polonsky. A language built around pattern matching on text.
description: David Farber, Ralph Griswold and Ivan Polonsky created SNOBOL at Bell Labs in 1962 for manipulating strings of text. Pattern matching was built into the language, far more powerful than the regular expressions of the time, and SNOBOL4 added associative tables. It was slow, and its control flow based on success and failure jumps was unusual. It was used in humanities computing and text processing, and its ideas passed to AWK, Icon and Perl.

name: T-SQL
outlook_would_change_if: SQL Server and Fabric warehouses moved logic out of stored procedures.
status_note: SQL Server, Azure SQL and Fabric keep it essential.
scope_text: Transact-SQL in Sybase and Microsoft SQL Server.
blurb: Sybase, later Microsoft. Procedural extensions to SQL for SQL Server.
description: Sybase created Transact-SQL (T-SQL) in 1987 for its SQL Server database, and Microsoft took it over when it licensed and later rewrote SQL Server. It adds variables, loops, error handling and stored procedures to SQL, so business logic can run inside the database next to the data. It is tied to Microsoft's (and Sybase's) databases, and procedural code inside a database is hard to test and version. It is used in Microsoft SQL Server, Azure SQL and Fabric warehouses for stored procedures, ETL jobs and reporting.
famous_software: SQL Server stored procedures (business logic in countless Microsoft-based companies); Fabric and Synapse warehouses (Microsoft's cloud data warehouses)

name: PL/SQL
outlook_would_change_if: Oracle's installed base migrated to other databases.
status_note: Oracle systems in banks and governments will run for decades.
blurb: Oracle. Procedural SQL with Ada-style syntax.
description: Oracle introduced PL/SQL in 1988 with Oracle 6 as a procedural extension to SQL, with syntax modeled on Ada. It adds blocks, variables, loops, exceptions and packages, so whole applications can run inside the Oracle database close to the data. It only runs on Oracle, and logic locked inside the database is hard to migrate and test. It is used in banks, telecoms and government systems built on Oracle, and in Oracle's own business applications.
famous_software: Oracle E-Business Suite (Oracle's own ERP applications); Oracle APEX apps (low-code web apps that run inside the database)

name: MDX
status_note: Replaced by tabular models and DAX; legacy cubes remain.
blurb: Microsoft. Queries for multidimensional OLAP cubes.
description: Microsoft created MDX (Multidimensional Expressions) in 1997, with Mosha Pasumansky as its lead architect, to query OLAP cubes in what became SQL Server Analysis Services. It extends SQL-like SELECT syntax to axes, hierarchies and members, so analysts can slice multidimensional data. It is notoriously hard to learn and has been displaced by tabular models and DAX. It still runs older Analysis Services cubes and the Excel pivot tables connected to them.
famous_software: Analysis Services cubes (multidimensional models behind Excel pivot tables)

name: Cypher
outlook_would_change_if: GQL fully absorbed Cypher (down), or graph databases became mainstream (up).
status_note: Graph databases and knowledge graphs grow, but the ISO GQL standard may absorb Cypher itself.
blurb: Neo4j. Pattern-based queries for graph databases.
description: Andrés Taylor and the team at Neo4j, a company founded in Malmö, Sweden, created Cypher in 2011 to query graph databases. Its patterns look like ASCII-art diagrams, (person)-[:KNOWS]->(friend), which makes relationships easy to read and query, and it became the basis of the ISO GQL standard in 2024. It only applies to graph data, and very large graph traversals can be slow. It is used for fraud detection, recommendation engines, knowledge graphs and network analysis.
famous_software: Neo4j applications (fraud detection, recommendations and knowledge graphs)

name: CPL
organization: University of Cambridge and University of London
designers: Christopher Strachey; David Barron; Cambridge–London team
designer_countries: United Kingdom; United Kingdom; United Kingdom (worked in)
status_note: Never fully implemented; BCPL is its legacy.
blurb: Cambridge and London, Christopher Strachey's team. An ambitious ALGOL 60 descendant, never fully implemented; BCPL is its stripped-down offspring.
description: Christopher Strachey's teams at the University of Cambridge and the University of London designed CPL (Combined Programming Language) from 1962 as a powerful successor to ALGOL 60 for both scientific and systems work.
