It was ambitious, with a rich type system and many features, and it proved very hard to implement: the project ran until 1966 without a complete compiler. Martin Richards removed 'all the difficult bits' to make BCPL, which is how CPL's ideas reached B and C. Its other legacy is vocabulary: the terms l-value and r-value come from Strachey's work around CPL.

name: ALGOL 68
designers: Adriaan van Wijngaarden; IFIP Working Group 2.1
status_note: Algol 68 Genie keeps it runnable; no new projects. Lives on through C, C++ and the Bourne shell.
blurb: IFIP Working Group 2.1, Adriaan van Wijngaarden. ALGOL's powerful, complex successor; gave C its type composition, C++ operator overloading and the Bourne shell if…fi.
description: IFIP Working Group 2.1, led by Adriaan van Wijngaarden, designed ALGOL 68 as the successor to ALGOL 60 and defined it with a new two-level grammar. It was orthogonal and powerful, with user-defined operators, references, unions and declarations anywhere in a block. Its report was famously hard to read, several committee members signed a minority report against it, and implementations were slow to arrive, so it never displaced ALGOL 60 or Pascal. Its ideas traveled further than the language: C's type composition, C++'s operator overloading and the Bourne shell's if…fi and case…esac all come from it.

name: ISWIM
organization: Univac Division of Sperry Rand, New York
status_note: A 'paperware' language that was never implemented as such; lives on in ML, Miranda and Haskell.
blurb: Peter Landin, 'The Next 700 Programming Languages'. A never-implemented 'paperware' language: expressions, let/where and the off-side rule.
description: Peter Landin described ISWIM ('If you See What I Mean') in his 1966 paper 'The Next 700 Programming Languages', written at Univac in New York. It was a family of languages built on the lambda calculus: everything is an expression, definitions use let and where, and indentation can show structure (Landin's 'off-side rule'). Landin presented it as an attempt to free LISP from its commitment to lists and its heavy bracketing. ISWIM itself was never implemented, but ML took its framework, David Turner's SASL, KRC and Miranda carried it to Haskell, and the off-side rule reappears in ABC and Python.

name: B
status_note: Replaced by C within a few years.
blurb: Bell Labs, Ken Thompson with Dennis Ritchie. BCPL squeezed onto the PDP-7; Ritchie added types and it became C.
description: Ken Thompson created B at Bell Labs around 1969 for the first Unix on the PDP-7, with Dennis Ritchie's help. Ritchie described it as 'BCPL squeezed into 8K bytes of memory and filtered through Thompson's brain': typeless, with the machine word as its only data type, and with compact operators such as ++ and --. On the byte-addressed PDP-11 the lack of types became a problem, so Ritchie added types and structures, and the result was C (1972). B was replaced within a few years, but much of C's look comes from it.

name: Common Lisp
organization: X3J13 committee (ANSI); 'Common Lisp the Language' by Guy Steele
designers: Guy Steele; Scott Fahlman; X3J13 committee
designer_countries: United States; United States; United States (worked in)
outlook_would_change_if: Macro-heavy, interactive Lisp development found new use with AI tooling.
status_note: SBCL is active and production systems exist (QPX, Grammarly), but the community is small.
blurb: Guy Steele and the X3J13 committee (ANSI 1994). Unified the Maclisp dialects; CLOS, macros and SBCL.
description: Common Lisp was designed from 1981 to unify the dialects that had grown out of Maclisp, with Guy Steele's book 'Common Lisp the Language' (1984) as its first reference and an ANSI standard following in 1994. It is a large, multi-paradigm language with powerful macros, a condition system and CLOS, an object system built on generic functions and multiple dispatch. Its size, its parentheses and a small job market limit adoption, and part of the Lisp community moved to Clojure. SBCL keeps it fast and active, and it runs ITA's airfare search (QPX, behind Google Flights), Grammarly's core engine and the first version of Reddit.
famous_software: ITA's QPX (the airfare search engine behind Orbitz and later Google Flights); Reddit (2005) (the first version, before a rewrite in Python); Grammarly (its core grammar engine runs on Common Lisp)

name: Cyclone
organization: AT&T Labs Research and Cornell University
designers: Trevor Jim; Greg Morrisett; AT&T Labs and Cornell team
designer_countries: United States (worked in); United States (worked in); United States (worked in)
status_note: Research project, inactive since 2006; its region ideas live on in Rust.
blurb: AT&T Labs and Cornell (Jim, Morrisett and others). A safe dialect of C with region-based memory; named in the Rust Reference.
description: Trevor Jim, Greg Morrisett and colleagues at AT&T Labs Research and Cornell University created Cyclone (2002) as a safe dialect of C. It kept C's syntax and low-level control but prevented buffer overflows, dangling pointers and format-string attacks, using fat pointers, tagged unions and region-based memory management checked by the compiler. It was a research language, harder to use than C, and development stopped around 2006. Its regions are a direct ancestor of Rust's lifetimes, and the Rust Reference lists it among Rust's influences.

name: Newsqueak
status_note: Superseded by Alef, Limbo and finally Go.
blurb: Bell Labs, Rob Pike. A concurrent language with channels as first-class values; its line (Alef, Limbo) led to Go.
description: Rob Pike designed Newsqueak at Bell Labs (published in 1989) to write interactive graphical programs, such as window systems, as sets of concurrent processes. Channels were first-class values: processes communicated by sending and receiving on them, in the style of Tony Hoare's CSP. It was an interpreted research language used mainly by Pike and his colleagues. Its ideas went into Alef and Limbo, Pike's later languages for Plan 9 and Inferno, and then into Go's goroutines and channels.

name: J
outlook_would_change_if: Array programming in plain ASCII caught on beyond its small community.
status_note: Jsoftware keeps it maintained and open source; a small community in finance, teaching and research.
blurb: Kenneth Iverson and Roger Hui. Iverson's ASCII successor to APL: the same array thinking, spelled with ordinary characters.
description: Kenneth Iverson and Roger Hui created J (1990, work beginning in 1989) as a successor to APL that uses ordinary ASCII characters instead of APL's special symbols. It keeps APL's array thinking and adds tacit programming, where functions are combined without naming their arguments. It is extremely concise but hard for outsiders to read, and its community is small. It is used in finance, teaching and research, and Jsoftware has made it open source.

name: K / q
outlook_would_change_if: Finance tick-data stacks moved to Python, Polars or DuckDB.
status_note: kdb+/q is entrenched in banks and trading firms for time-series data.
scope_text: K (1992) and q (2003), Whitney's closely related pair; q is a query layer written in K.
blurb: Arthur Whitney; Kx Systems. K (1992) is a terse ASCII array language; q (2003) adds a query layer and runs the kdb+ database.
description: Arthur Whitney, who had built APL systems at Morgan Stanley, created K in 1992 as a terse array language that replaces APL's special characters with ASCII. q (2003) adds readable keywords and a SQL-like query layer on top of K, and with it the kdb+ column-store database of Kx Systems, which Whitney co-founded. It is extremely fast on time-series data but famously cryptic, proprietary and expensive, with a small, highly paid talent pool. It runs tick-data and trading analytics at many banks and trading firms.
famous_software: kdb+ tick databases (time-series databases used by banks and trading firms)

name: VBA
outlook_would_change_if: Microsoft retired VBA (down), or Office Scripts and Python in Excel stalled (up).
status_note: Still behind countless Excel and Access tools, but Microsoft no longer evolves it.
blurb: Microsoft (Excel 5, 1993). Visual Basic embedded in Office: the macro language behind countless Excel and Access tools.
description: Microsoft introduced Visual Basic for Applications in Excel 5 (1993) to give Office a common macro language based on Visual Basic. Users can record macros and then edit the code behind them, automating workbooks, Access databases and other Office applications. It is old, Windows-centric and a common security risk, and Microsoft has stopped evolving it in favor of Office Scripts (TypeScript) and Python in Excel. It still runs countless business tools, reports and financial models.
famous_software: Excel and Access macros (automation in countless business workbooks)
